meta.title: Skeletal Muscle
meta.summary: Muscle is the body's engine: it is the only tissue that converts chemical energy (ATP) into physical pulling force.

sections.title: Skeletal Muscle Structure — From Whole Muscle to Molecule
Myofibrils and the Sarcomere — Why Muscle Looks Striped
The Molecular Players — Thick and Thin Filaments
Fueling Contraction — Where the Energy Comes From

items: Muscle is the body's engine: it is the only tissue that converts chemical energy (ATP) into physical pulling force.
Skeletal muscle is built like Russian dolls: whole muscle → bundles (fascicles) → cells (fibres) → myofibrils → sarcomeres. Each level is just the level above, bundled.
The central surprise: the filaments never shorten. They slide past each other, like interlocking your fingers and pulling your hands together.
Two switches run everything — calcium turns contraction on, ATP makes it move (and lets it stop). Almost every fact in this topic hangs off those two.
Muscle does five jobs: movement, posture, joint stability, heat production, and moving substances through the body.
Four defining properties: excitability (responds to signals), contractility (can shorten), extensibility (can be stretched), elasticity (springs back).
By control: voluntary (skeletal) or involuntary (cardiac, smooth). By appearance: striated (skeletal, cardiac) or non-striated (smooth).
Combine the two and you get the three types: skeletal = striated + voluntary; cardiac = striated + involuntary; smooth = non-striated + involuntary.
Shivering is muscle deliberately contracting for heat rather than movement — proof that heat production is a real job, not a by-product.
Standing still is not 'doing nothing': dozens of postural muscles are working continuously to stop you folding up.

blocks.x: Muscle is the only tissue in your body that can deliberately shorten itself and pull on something. That single ability — contraction — is why you can walk, why your heart beats, and why food moves through your gut.

blocks.name: Muscle (general description)
blocks.def: A very specialized tissue with the ability to BOTH contract AND conduct electrical impulses. Muscle is very well supplied with blood vessels, nerves, and other neural tissue — it's metabolically hungry and needs constant support.

blocks.name: Five main functions of muscle
blocks.def: Maintain body posture, stabilize joints, produce movement, generate heat, and guard entrances and exits (sphincters).

blocks.name: Four characteristics of muscle tissue
blocks.def: Stretchability, elasticity, irritability (excitability), and the ability to develop tension.

blocks.name: Functional classification of muscle
blocks.def: Voluntary (under conscious control) versus involuntary (not under conscious control).

blocks.name: Structural classification of muscle
blocks.def: Striated (shows visible banding) versus smooth (no visible banding).

blocks.name: The three muscle types, combining both classifications
blocks.def: Striated voluntary (skeletal) muscle, generally attached to the skeleton; smooth involuntary (smooth) muscle, found primarily in tubular organs; and striated involuntary (cardiac) muscle, found in the wall of the heart. Notice cardiac muscle is the 'odd one out' — striated like skeletal, but involuntary like smooth.

sections.title: Skeletal Muscle Structure — From Whole Muscle to Molecule

items: Think of an electrical cable: outer sheath, bundles of wires inside, each wire itself made of thin strands.
Epimysium wraps the whole muscle → perimysium wraps each bundle (fascicle) → endomysium wraps each individual fibre.
One muscle fibre = one cell, but an unusual one: long, cylindrical, and multinucleated (many nuclei), because it forms by many cells fusing.
Inside each fibre are hundreds of myofibrils, and each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres — the actual contracting units.
Those connective-tissue layers are not just packaging: they merge at the ends to form the tendon, which is how the pull reaches bone.
The visible 'grain' in a piece of meat you are cutting is the fascicles — you can literally see this anatomy on your plate.
Tendon injuries are slow to heal because tendon is dense connective tissue with a poor blood supply, unlike the muscle it serves.

blocks.x: Picture a thick rope. The whole rope is the muscle; inside it are bundles of strands; inside each bundle are individual threads; and inside each thread are even finer fibers. Skeletal muscle is organized exactly this way, wrapped in connective tissue at every single level.

blocks.name: Skeletal muscle (definition)
blocks.def: Striated, voluntary muscle, usually attached to bone by tendons made of connective tissue.

blocks.name: Epimysium
blocks.def: The connective tissue sheath surrounding the ENTIRE muscle — the outermost wrapping.

blocks.name: Fascicles (fasciculi)
blocks.def: The numerous subunits or bundles that a skeletal muscle is divided into, each surrounded by its own connective tissue called perimysium.

blocks.name: Perimysium
blocks.def: The connective tissue surrounding each individual fascicle (bundle of muscle fibers).

blocks.name: Muscle fiber (muscle cell)
blocks.def: The individual cell that makes up a fascicle; each one is ensheathed by its own connective tissue layer called the endomysium.

blocks.name: Endomysium
blocks.def: The connective tissue surrounding each individual muscle fiber — the innermost wrapping, right against the cell itself.

blocks.name: Myofibrils
blocks.def: The many fibrils found within each muscle cell/fiber — essentially bundles of contractile protein filaments packed inside the cell.

blocks.name: Myofilaments
blocks.def: The long protein molecules that myofibrils are made of. There are two types: thick and thin myofilaments — these are the actual force-generating machinery.

blocks.name: Skeletal muscle fiber shape
blocks.def: Elongated, unbranched, and cylindrical.

blocks.name: Skeletal muscle fiber nuclei
blocks.def: Multinucleated, with the nuclei located peripherally — just under the <term d="The straw-coloured liquid part of blood that carries the cells, proteins, nutrients and wastes.">plasma</term> membrane (<term d="The cell membrane of a muscle fibre.">sarcolemma</term>) — leaving the central part of the fiber free for myofibrils.

blocks.title: Next up — the fibre's own named parts

items: Muscle renames the standard cell parts: sarcolemma = cell membrane, sarcoplasm = cytoplasm. (Sarco- simply means flesh.)
T tubules are inward folds of the membrane that carry the electrical signal deep inside the fibre.
Terminal cisternae are the calcium stores sitting beside them; one T tubule + two cisternae = a triad.
Why this matters: without it, only the outer shell of the fibre would contract. The triad is what makes the whole fibre fire together.

blocks.name: Sarcolemma
blocks.def: The plasma membrane of a muscle fiber — the muscle-specific name for what would just be 'the cell membrane' in any other cell.

blocks.name: Sarcoplasm
blocks.def: The cytoplasm of a muscle fiber, containing the myofibrils, mitochondria, enzymes, and other cell contents.

blocks.name: <term d="The muscle cell's internal calcium store, released to trigger contraction.">Sarcoplasmic reticulum</term> (SR)
blocks.def: A structure that envelops each <term d="A long bundle of contractile filaments packed inside a muscle fibre.">myofibril</term>; its primary function is to STORE calcium ions, ready for release when contraction is triggered.

blocks.name: T tubules (transverse tubules)
blocks.def: Formed by invaginations of the sarcolemma, running transverse (crosswise) to the myofibrils. Their function is to conduct electrical impulses from the cell surface DOWN INTO the cell, specifically to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. T tubules are extensions of the sarcolemma and are filled with <term d="All the body fluid sitting outside the cells, including blood plasma and the fluid bathing tissues.">extracellular fluid</term> (ECF), since they're topologically continuous with the outside of the cell.

blocks.name: Terminal cisternae
blocks.def: The enlarged ends of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which make contact with the T tubules.

blocks.name: Triad
blocks.def: The structure formed where a T tubule is flanked by two terminal cisternae (one on each side), located at the A-I band junction — the physical meeting point where the electrical signal (in the T tubule) gets handed off to the calcium-storing SR.

sections.title: Myofibrils and the Sarcomere — Why Muscle Looks Striped

items: The stripes are an optical illusion of overlap — dark where thick and thin filaments overlap, light where only thin filaments sit.
A band = dark, the full length of the thick filament (it never changes length). I band = light, thin filaments only.
Z line anchors the thin filaments and marks the boundary: one sarcomere = Z line to Z line. M line holds the thick filaments in the middle. H band = thick filaments with no overlap.
The tell-tale of contraction: the I band and H band shrink, but the A band never does — proof that filaments slide rather than shorten.
Titin is a giant elastic protein running from Z line to M line — the built-in spring that stops overstretch and recoils the sarcomere.
Titin behaves like the elastic in a waistband: it lets things stretch, then pulls them back and prevents damage from overstretching.

blocks.name: Two types of myofilaments in a myofibril
blocks.def: Thick and thin myofilaments, arranged in a precise, repeating pattern that gives the muscle cell its characteristic striped (striated) appearance under the microscope.

blocks.name: Why striations appear
blocks.def: The striations arise because of DIFFERENCES IN REFRACTIVE INDEX between the thick and thin filaments — light bends differently passing through each, creating visible light and dark bands.

blocks.name: A band (anisotropic band)
blocks.def: The band formed by the THICK filaments — appears dark.

blocks.name: I band (isotropic band)
blocks.def: The band formed by the THIN filaments — appears light.

blocks.name: H band
blocks.def: A lighter band WITHIN the A band, representing the region where there is NO overlap between thick and thin filaments (only thick filaments alone).

blocks.name: M line
blocks.def: A dark line within the H band, representing proteins that connect adjacent thick filaments to each other, holding them in register.

blocks.name: Z line (Z disc)
blocks.def: A dark line running through each I band, connecting adjacent thin filaments together. This is the structural boundary marker of a sarcomere.

blocks.name: Sarcomere
blocks.def: The unit running from one Z line to the next — the functional, contractile unit of a muscle. Every contraction is, at the microscopic level, thousands of sarcomeres shortening simultaneously.

blocks.name: Filament overlap ratio
blocks.def: Each thick myofilament is always surrounded by 6 thin myofilaments; conversely, each thin myofilament is surrounded by 3 thick myofilaments — a precise, fixed geometric relationship.

blocks.name: Titin (connectin)
blocks.def: A giant protein within the sarcomere that anchors at the Z-disc and extends all the way to the M-line. Titin acts as a molecular spring and is the main source of PASSIVE elasticity in muscle — it's why a relaxed muscle still resists being over-stretched, even with no active contraction happening.

sections.title: The Molecular Players — Thick and Thin Filaments

items: Thick filament = myosin, shaped like a golf club. Its heads are the crossbridges — the parts that actually grab and pull.
Thin filament = actin, plus two regulatory proteins riding on it: tropomyosin and troponin.
Tropomyosin is the cover: at rest it lies across actin's binding sites so myosin cannot attach. This is why a resting muscle stays relaxed.
Troponin is the switch with three parts: TnT binds tropomyosin, TnI inhibits (holds the cover in place), TnC binds calcium.
So the trigger is simple: calcium binds TnC → the cover slides aside → myosin can grab actin.
Troponin is not just theory — a blood troponin test is the standard way a heart attack is diagnosed. Damaged heart muscle leaks troponin into the blood.

blocks.name: Thick myofilaments
blocks.def: Composed of the protein <term d="The thick filament protein whose heads pull on actin to shorten the muscle.">myosin</term>. Each myosin molecule has a tail (forming the core of the thick filament) plus two heads that project outward from the core.

blocks.name: Myosin heads (crossbridges)
blocks.def: The projecting heads of myosin molecules, commonly called crossbridges. Key characteristics: they have an ATP-binding site that functions as an ATPase, an actin-binding site, and a flexible 'hinge' where the head leaves the core of the thick filament.

blocks.name: Thin myofilaments
blocks.def: Composed of THREE types of protein: <term d="The thin filament protein that the thick filaments grab and pull on during contraction.">actin</term>, troponin, and tropomyosin — a three-protein team, not just actin alone.

blocks.name: Actin
blocks.def: Spherical protein molecules that form long chains; each thin filament contains TWO such chains twisted into a double helix. Actin molecules carry the binding sites for myosin — the docking points the crossbridges will eventually attach to.

blocks.name: Tropomyosin
blocks.def: A long protein filament that entwines around the actin filament. In a RELAXED muscle, tropomyosin physically BLOCKS the myosin-binding sites on actin, preventing contraction — think of it as a security gate covering the docking ports.

blocks.name: Troponin
blocks.def: A small globular protein complex connected to tropomyosin at regular intervals, made of three subunits: Troponin T, Troponin I, and Troponin C.

blocks.name: Troponin T (TnT)
blocks.def: Binds to tropomyosin, interlocking with it to form the troponin-tropomyosin complex.

blocks.name: Troponin I (TnI)
blocks.def: Binds to actin, holding the troponin-tropomyosin complex in place on the thin filament.

blocks.name: Troponin C (TnC)
blocks.def: Binds to CALCIUM ions — when Ca2+ binds TnC, it produces a conformational change in TnI, which is the trigger that ultimately moves tropomyosin out of the way. TnC is the calcium sensor of the whole contraction machine.

items: Three steps overall: excitation (electrical signal arrives) → coupling (signal releases calcium) → contraction (filaments slide).

Excitation–contraction coupling is the crucial link: the action potential runs down the T-tubules into the depths of the fibre, where DHPRs sense the voltage and mechanically open the ryanodine receptors, dumping calcium out of storage.

The crossbridge cycle, in four beats: (1) ATP is split, cocking the myosin head → (2) the head attaches to actin → (3) the power stroke pulls the thin filament inward → (4) a fresh ATP binds and the head lets go.
That cycle repeats many times per second — a molecular ratchet, hauling in rope hand over hand.
Note ATP is needed twice: once to cock the head, and again to release it. That second requirement explains rigor mortis.
Rowing a boat: the oar catches the water, pulls, releases, and reaches forward again — each myosin head is one oar, and thousands row together.
Because the T-tubule system carries the signal deep inside, the whole fibre contracts at once rather than just its surface.

blocks.x: Contraction is a three-act play: first the nerve tells the muscle to fire (excitation), then that electrical signal gets translated into a chemical trigger inside the cell (<term d="The chain of events linking the electrical signal at the membrane to the actual mechanical contraction.">excitation-contraction coupling</term>), and finally the actual molecular machinery does its ratcheting work (the sliding filament mechanism).

blocks.name: Three main events in skeletal muscle contraction
blocks.def: Electrical excitation of the muscle fiber, excitation-contraction coupling, and muscle fiber contraction via the sliding filament mechanism — in that order, each one triggering the next.

blocks.name: Electrical excitation of a muscle fiber
blocks.def: Skeletal muscle fibers can be stimulated by a motor neuron (in the body) or a voltage stimulator (in a lab). <term d="The difference in electrical charge between the inside and outside of a cell membrane.">Resting membrane potentialThe steady negative charge inside a cell while it is not firing.</term> is about -90 mV. <term d="A shift of the membrane potential toward zero — the inside of the cell becomes less negative.">Depolarization</term> starts at the motor end plate; if it reaches <term d="The minimum strength of stimulus needed to trigger an action potential.">threshold</term>, an <term d="A brief, all-or-nothing electrical signal that sweeps along a nerve or muscle cell.">action potential</term> is initiated.

blocks.name: Excitation-contraction coupling (definition)
blocks.def: The process by which depolarization of the muscle fiber initiates contraction — the crucial link between an electrical event and a mechanical one.

blocks.name: Excitation-contraction coupling — the steps
blocks.def: The action potential travels along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules. The voltage change is sensed by dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs), voltage-dependent calcium channels in the T-tubule membrane. DHPRs undergo a conformational change and open ryanodine receptors (RyRs) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, to which they're mechanically coupled. Opening the RyRs releases Ca2+ from the SR into the sarcoplasm. This Ca2+ binds Troponin C, causing troponin to change shape and pull tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin — finally exposing the docking sites.

blocks.name: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs)
blocks.def: Voltage-dependent calcium channels located in the T-tubule membrane that sense the arriving action potential's voltage change and mechanically trigger the ryanodine receptors on the SR.

blocks.name: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs)
blocks.def: Calcium release channels located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Once opened (triggered by DHPRs), they release the SR's stored Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm — the actual calcium-release step of excitation-contraction coupling.

blocks.title: Next up — the four-beat cycle, in order

items: Read the next four definitions as one repeating loop, not four separate facts.
Cock → attach → pull → release, then straight back to cock.
ATP appears twice: once to cock the head, once to release it. Miss that and rigor mortis makes no sense.
The cycle repeats as long as calcium is present and ATP is available — remove either and contraction stops.

blocks.name: The four steps of crossbridge cycling
blocks.def: ATP hydrolysis, attachment of myosin to actin (forming crosslinkages), the power stroke, and detachment of myosin from actin — this four-step cycle repeats over and over during a contraction.

blocks.name: Step 1: ATP hydrolysis
blocks.def: ATP binds to the ATP-binding site on the crossbridge; the ATPase hydrolyzes it into ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi). This energizes the myosin head and INCREASES its affinity for actin. Part of the energy released is lost as heat (which is exactly why exercising muscle generates body heat).

blocks.name: Step 2: Attachment (crosslinkage formation)
blocks.def: The now energized myosin head binds to the newly-unblocked myosin-binding site on actin, and Pi is released from the myosin head.

blocks.name: Step 3: Power stroke
blocks.def: Release of Pi starts the power stroke — the myosin head rotates, pulling the thin filament toward the center of the sarcomere. ADP is released from the myosin head during this stroke, but the head STAYS attached to actin throughout.

blocks.name: Step 4: Detachment
blocks.def: A fresh ATP molecule binds the myosin ATP-binding site, decreasing the crossbridge's affinity for actin. The crossbridge detaches from actin, and the whole cycle begins again — as long as calcium and ATP remain available.

blocks.name: Why the contraction cycle keeps going
blocks.def: The contraction cycle continues for as long as intracellular calcium levels remain high — the fiber contracts because the thin filaments (actin) slide past the thick filaments (myosin). Each individual crossbridge cycle shortens the muscle fiber by only about 1% of its resting length — full contraction requires this cycle to repeat thousands of times.

items: The core claim: filaments do not shorten — they slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens while the filaments stay the same length.
Evidence sits in the bands: I and H bands narrow; the A band is unchanged.
Requirements: calcium to unlock, ATP to power, and an intact overlap between thick and thin filaments.
Interlock your fingers and slide your hands together — your fingers do not get shorter, but the gap closes. That is a sarcomere contracting.
It is also why a telescope is such a good analogy: overall length changes, individual segments do not.

blocks.cap: Relaxed vs contracted sarcomere — filaments overlap more, they don’t shrink.

blocks.name: Sliding-filament theory
blocks.def: The explanation for how muscles produce force and (usually) shorten. The thick and thin filaments within the sarcomere SLIDE PAST one another, via the repeated breaking and reforming of actin-myosin crosslinkages. As the filaments slide, the Z lines approach each other, decreasing the width of the sarcomere.

blocks.name: Key insight of the sliding filament theory
blocks.def: Although the WIDTH of the sarcomere changes during contraction, the LENGTHS of the individual filaments themselves do NOT change — filaments don't shrink, they simply overlap more. The changing width is purely a consequence of how much the filaments overlap, not any change in filament length.

blocks.name: Requirements for sliding filament contraction
blocks.def: This mechanism can only occur when there is sufficient calcium (Ca2+) present AND sufficient ATP available — remove either one and contraction cannot proceed.

items: Relaxation is an active, energy-consuming process, not simply switching off: calcium must be pumped back into storage using ATP.
Once calcium falls, tropomyosin slides back over the binding sites and the muscle goes slack.
Rigor is what happens with no ATP at all: myosin heads attach to actin and cannot let go, because release requires a fresh ATP. The muscle locks solid.
Rigor mortis after death is exactly this — ATP production stops, the crossbridges lock, and the body stiffens until the proteins themselves break down.
It also explains a counterintuitive fact worth remembering: you need energy to relax, not just to contract.

blocks.name: Muscle relaxation
blocks.def: Occurs when Ca2+ is actively pumped BACK into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by Ca2+-ATPase. When intracellular Ca2+ falls below about 10^-7 M around the myofibrils, Ca2+ is removed from troponin, tropomyosin reverts to its blocking conformation, and contraction ceases.

blocks.name: Rigor
blocks.def: A state of extreme rigidity caused by depletion of BOTH ATP and creatine phosphate in skeletal muscle cells. When this occurs after death, it is called rigor mortis — the myosin heads get stuck attached to actin because there's no ATP left to trigger detachment.

sections.title: Fueling Contraction — Where the Energy Comes From

items: ATP is the only currency muscle accepts, but the stored amount lasts only a few seconds — so it must be regenerated continuously.
Creatine phosphate — the instant top-up. Fastest, but exhausted in roughly 10–15 seconds.
Glycolysis — fast, needs no oxygen, but yields little ATP and produces lactic acid. Good for around a minute or two of hard effort.
Oxidative phosphorylation — slow to ramp up, needs oxygen, but produces far more ATP and can run for hours.
The three are not rivals; they are a relay team, each handing over as the previous one fades.
A 100 m sprint runs almost entirely on stored ATP and creatine phosphate — which is exactly why nobody can sprint flat out for a minute.
A long walk or a marathon runs on oxidative phosphorylation — slower, but essentially inexhaustible while fuel and oxygen last.
That burning feeling in a long climb of stairs is the glycolytic middle gear doing the work.

blocks.name: ATP as the immediate energy source
blocks.def: ATP is the immediate energy source for ALL muscle contractions. However, ATP stores in the muscle can only sustain contraction for about 3 seconds on their own — the muscle must constantly regenerate ATP from other sources during any sustained activity.

blocks.name: Three sources for regenerating ATP in muscle
blocks.def: Creatine phosphate (the phosphagen system), glycogen (via glycolysis), and cellular respiration in the mitochondria (oxidative phosphorylation) — these three systems activate roughly in sequence as a contraction is sustained longer.

blocks.name: Creatine phosphate system
blocks.def: The pool of creatine phosphate in a fiber is about 10 times larger than the ATP pool, serving as a modest reservoir. Creatine phosphate directly phosphorylates ADP to ATP (Creatine phosphate + ADP ↔ Creatine + ATP), a reaction catalyzed by creatine phosphoryltransferase. Called 'alactic anaerobic' because it neither produces lactate nor requires oxygen. Can sustain contraction for about 5-8 seconds.

blocks.name: Glycogen (glycolysis) system
blocks.def: Kicks in after creatine phosphate is depleted, sustaining contraction for up to about 1 minute. Skeletal muscle fibers contain about 1% glycogen; glycogenolysis produces glucose-1-phosphate, which enters glycolysis, ending in pyruvate and ATP. Without oxygen, pyruvate converts to lactic acid ('fast glycolysis,' producing little ATP quickly, and this source fails once glycogen is depleted — fibers relying on this fatigue quickly). Called 'lactic anaerobic' because it produces lactate without requiring oxygen. WITH oxygen present, pyruvate instead converts to acetyl-CoA and is fully metabolized via the Krebs cycle ('slow glycolysis').

blocks.name: Cellular respiration (oxidative phosphorylation)
blocks.def: Required to meet the ATP needs of muscle engaged in PROLONGED activity. Much slower than the other two systems, but generates ATP continuously and efficiently — fibers relying on it take longer to fatigue. Substrates are primarily glucose and free fatty acids. All three energy systems are active at all times, but the relative contribution of each shifts depending on exercise intensity and duration.

items: A muscle behaves like a motor with springs attached: the contractile elements generate force, while series and parallel elastic elements (tendons, titin, connective sheaths) store and smooth it.
Isotonic = the muscle changes length and moves a load. Concentric = shortening while pulling; eccentric = lengthening while still resisting.
Eccentric work is the muscle acting as a brake rather than a motor — controlling a movement instead of causing it.
Lifting a bag to the table is concentric; lowering it slowly is eccentric.
Walking downhill or down stairs is mostly eccentric work — and it is why going down leaves you sorer the next day than going up.

blocks.name: Contractile elements (CE)
blocks.def: The contractile fibrils actually responsible for muscle contraction — these SHORTEN during contraction.

blocks.name: Series Elastic Elements (SEE)
blocks.def: Elastic elements found outside or inside the muscle, arranged IN SERIES with the contractile elements — they allow a contracted muscle to reach a length greater than its original resting length when actively stretched, and they LENGTHEN slightly during contraction. Examples: tendon, titin.

blocks.name: Parallel Elastic Elements (PEE)
blocks.def: Elastic elements provided by muscle membranes/connective tissue, arranged IN PARALLEL with the contractile elements — they produce tension only when a muscle is passively stretched past its resting length, and they REMAIN AT THE SAME LENGTH during contraction. Examples: connective tissue of the muscle, endomysium, perimysium, epimysium.

blocks.name: <term d="A contraction where the muscle develops tension but its length does not change.">Isometric</term> contraction
blocks.def: The muscle develops force but does NOT shorten — no visible movement occurs (e.g., pushing against an immovable wall). The force developed equals the load being contracted against, due to the presence of the muscle's elastic components.

blocks.name: <term d="A contraction where the muscle shortens while the load on it stays the same.">Isotonic</term> contraction
blocks.def: The muscle generates a CONSTANT force to move a load — there are two types: concentric and eccentric.

blocks.name: Concentric isotonic contraction
blocks.def: The muscle SHORTENS as it contracts, because the force generated is sufficient to overcome the resistance. The force generated is always less than the muscle's absolute maximum, and contraction velocity is determined by the load. Example: raising a weight during a bicep curl.

blocks.name: Eccentric isotonic contraction
blocks.def: The force generated is INSUFFICIENT to overcome the external load, so the muscle LENGTHENS even as it contracts. Example: the controlled downward (lowering) movement of a dumbbell during a bicep curl.

items: A motor unit = one motor neuron plus every fibre it commands. Small units (a few fibres) give fine control; large units give power.
A single stimulus produces a twitch, with three phases: latent (nothing visible yet — coupling is happening), contraction, and relaxation.
Wave summation: if a second stimulus arrives before relaxation is complete, the contractions stack and grow stronger.
Stimulate fast enough and twitches fuse into tetanus — incomplete (bumpy) or complete (smooth, maximal).
This is how force is graded: fire faster, and recruit more motor units. Real movements are smooth because units take turns rather than all firing together.
Threading a needle uses tiny motor units in the hand; lifting a bag of cement uses huge ones in the thigh and back. Same principle, different unit size.
Your movements never look like a series of separate jerks because almost all normal contraction is fused tetanus.

blocks.name: <term d="One motor neuron together with every muscle fibre it supplies.">Motor unit</term>
blocks.def: A single motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates. A motor neuron stimulates ALL the muscle fibers in its motor unit simultaneously — they act as one functional group.

blocks.name: Factors determining a motor unit's force output
blocks.def: The number of muscle fibers within the motor unit, the size of the individual muscle cells, the initial length of the fibers at rest, and the number of crossbridges attached to actin.

blocks.name: Muscle twitch
blocks.def: The quick shortening seen in a skeletal muscle when a SINGLE action potential (traveling down a motor neuron) stimulates the motor unit's fibers to contract once. The minimal stimulus producing a twitch is called the threshold stimulus.

blocks.x: ▶️Twitch, Summation and <term d="A smooth, sustained contraction produced when stimuli arrive too fast for the muscle to relax in between.">Tetanus</term>Video · Non Stop Neurone

blocks.name: Three phases of a muscle twitch
blocks.def: Latent period, contraction period, and relaxation period, in that order.

blocks.name: Latent period (of a twitch)
blocks.def: Lasts about 2 msec — the time between stimulation and force generation, corresponding to the time required for Ca2+ release.

blocks.name: Contraction period (of a twitch)
blocks.def: Lasts about 10-100 msec — the period during which force is increasing.

blocks.name: Relaxation period (of a twitch)
blocks.def: Lasts about 10-100 msec — the period during which force decreases and the muscle returns to its original length, corresponding to the time Ca2+ takes to be actively pumped back into the SR.

blocks.title: Next up — how single twitches become real force

items: A twitch on its own is useless — far too weak and too brief for any real movement.
The trick is timing: fire again before relaxation finishes and the contractions stack.
Stack them fast enough and they fuse into tetanus — smooth, sustained, maximal force.
Nearly every movement you make today will be fused tetanus, not individual twitches.

blocks.name: Wave summation
blocks.def: If muscle fibers of a motor unit are re-stimulated BEFORE the relaxation phase of the previous twitch is complete, the next contraction produces a GREATER force than the first. Possible because contraction and relaxation phases last much longer than the <term d="A short spell straight after firing when the cell cannot fire again, or needs a stronger stimulus.">refractory period</term>, so with rapid stimulation there's little time to clear all the Ca2+ from the sarcoplasm — more Ca2+ present means more active crosslinkages form, and therefore a stronger contraction.

blocks.name: Tetanus
blocks.def: If a muscle fiber is stimulated so rapidly that it does NOT relax at all between stimuli, a smooth, sustained maximal contraction called tetanus occurs.

blocks.name: Incomplete (unfused) tetanus
blocks.def: Occurs when there is PARTIAL relaxation between successive muscle twitches — the contraction is strong and sustained but still shows small dips.

blocks.name: Complete (fused) tetanus
blocks.def: Occurs when there is NO relaxation observed between twitches at all — a perfectly smooth, sustained contraction. The tension developed during complete tetanus is about 4 TIMES that of a single twitch.

blocks.name: Treppe (staircase phenomenon)
blocks.def: A gradual INCREASE in the extent of muscular contraction following rapid, repeated stimulation at a frequency slightly BELOW the tetanizing frequency. Believed to be due to increased availability of Ca2+ for troponin binding as stimulation continues.

items: Type I (slow oxidative) — slow, fatigue-resistant, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, red. Built for endurance and posture.
Type IIa (fast oxidative) — the middle ground: fast but reasonably fatigue-resistant.
Type IIb (fast glycolytic) — fast, powerful, tires quickly, pale. Built for bursts.
Length–tension relationship: a muscle produces maximum force at an optimal length, where thick–thin overlap is ideal.
Too short and the filaments collide and interfere; too stretched and there are too few crossbridges able to attach. Either way, force falls.
Total tension = active (crossbridges) + passive (elastic recoil).
Chicken meat makes it visible: dark leg meat (Type I — standing all day) versus pale breast meat (Type II — short powerful bursts of flapping).
You cannot grip strongly with a fully clenched or fully splayed hand — grip is strongest at a middle position, which is the length–tension curve in your own hand.
It also explains why athletes 'load up' — coiling into a crouch before jumping puts muscles near optimal length.

blocks.name: Three skeletal muscle fiber types
blocks.def: Type I, Type IIa, and Type IIb — classified based on twitch duration, and differing in structure and biochemistry. Most skeletal muscles contain a MIX of all three types, but any single motor unit is always made of ONE type only, never a mixture.

blocks.name: Type I fibers (Slow Oxidative)
blocks.def: Loaded with mitochondria, depend on cellular respiration for ATP, highly resistant to fatigue, rich in myoglobin (hence RED in color), have extensive blood supply, activated by small-diameter (slow-conducting) motor neurons, small fiber size, and are dominant in muscles responsible for POSTURE (which must work continuously without tiring).

blocks.name: Type IIa fibers (Fast Oxidative / fatigue-resistant)
blocks.def: Red fibers, rich in myoglobin, with many mitochondria and an extensive capillary network. Depend on BOTH cellular respiration and glycolysis for ATP, and are moderately resistant to fatigue — needed for sports like middle-distance running and swimming, where you need speed AND some endurance.

blocks.name: Type IIb fibers (Fast Glycolytic)
blocks.def: Few mitochondria, rich in glycogen, depend on glycolysis for ATP, fatigue EASILY, low in myoglobin (hence whitish/pale), activated by large-diameter (fast-conducting) motor neurons, less extensive blood supply, extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum, larger fiber size, and dominant in muscles used for RAPID, powerful movement (like a sprint or a jump).

blocks.name: Length-tension relationship (overview)
blocks.def: The force developed by a muscle — whether contracting or resting — is strongly dependent on the length of the muscle at the time. Force exerted depends on the number of myosin heads pulling together at the same time.

blocks.name: Passive tension curve
blocks.def: A plot of the tension developed when a muscle is stretched to different lengths WITHOUT stimulation — this passive tension is attributed to the elasticity of the muscle's elastic elements, chiefly the protein titin.

blocks.name: Total tension curve
blocks.def: A plot of the peak tetanic tension developed at different lengths DURING stimulation — this reflects the combined contribution of both the contractile AND elastic elements.

blocks.name: Active tension curve
blocks.def: Obtained by SUBTRACTING the passive tension curve from the total tension curve — isolating the contribution from the contractile elements alone.

blocks.name: Why tension varies with sarcomere length
blocks.def: At SHORT sarcomere lengths, low active tension develops because thin filaments from either side of the M-line interfere with (crash into) each other. At LONG sarcomere lengths, low tension develops because filament overlap is too restricted. MAXIMAL tension develops at the length allowing maximum overlap WITHOUT interference — this length is called the resting (optimal) length.

blocks.name: Why the length-tension relationship matters conceptually
blocks.def: This relationship helps verify the hypothesis that crosslinkages between actin and myosin generate the contractile tension, and directly supports the sliding filament theory — the amount of force a muscle can produce is a direct, measurable consequence of how much its filaments can physically overlap.

items: A band is Always the same length; I band shrInks; H band sHrinks.
Z to Z = one sarcomere.
Calcium unlocks it; ATP powers it. If a question asks 'what starts contraction?' the answer is calcium binding troponin C.
Cock → attach → pull → release, and ATP is needed at both the first and last step.
Slow = red = endurance (Type I); fast = pale = bursts (Type II).

blocks.title: Cleared up — the confusions that cost marks

items: The filaments do not shorten. They slide. The sarcomere shortens, the filaments never do.
Relaxation costs ATP too. That is not a detail — it is the entire explanation of rigor mortis.
'Tetanus' here means fused contraction, not the disease caused by Clostridium tetani.
More force ≠ bigger action potentials. Force is graded by firing rate and motor unit recruitment.
Eccentric contraction is still contraction — the muscle is lengthening while actively resisting, not relaxing.
← Excitable Tissues (Topic 03): the action potential you learned there is what arrives here. Muscle is simply another excitable tissue, with a contractile machine bolted on.
← Body Fluids (Topic 01): calcium storage and release, and the pumps that reclaim it, are membrane transport in action.
→ Cardiac & Smooth Muscle (Topics 05–06): both reuse this same sliding-filament machinery — what changes is where calcium comes from, and who gives the orders.
→ Communication Between Cells (Topic 07): the neuromuscular junction is the exact handover point where nerve becomes muscle.
The one-line summary: calcium unlocks it, ATP powers it, filaments slide — and force is graded by how often and how many.

mnemonics.h: A band Always, I band Isn't
lines: In contraction the A band keeps its length while the I band and H zone shorten — the filaments slide, they do not shrink.
Calcium binds troponin C, which drags tropomyosin off the actin binding sites and lets the cross-bridge cycle begin.
One to cock and power the stroke, one to detach myosin from actin — no ATP means no detachment, which is exactly rigor mortis.
Type I fibres are oxidative, myoglobin-rich and fatigue-resistant; type II are glycolytic, faster and quicker to fatigue.
